skill.name: devrel-strategy
skill.description: Designs a company's developer relations program from the top - the business driver that funds it, the two goals it is allowed to serve, the pillar mix (advocacy, marketing, enablement, community) for its stage, audience priority, build-vs-buy per bet, staffing sequence, and a written refused list. Use whenever someone asks whether to start doing DevRel, what a new devrel program should do first, why devrel work is busy but not landing, how to justify the program to an exec, which pillar deserves the next investment, who to hire next, or whether to outsource content, events or community - even if they never say "strategy". Not the first-90-days plan - use samber/developer-relations-skills@developer-relations-kickoff. Not metrics, org chart or budget math.
skill.summary: Build a developer relations charter with funded goals, audience priorities, sourcing choices, staffing triggers, and explicit exclusions.
skill.author: samber

content.user_title: Design a Focused Developer Relations Charter
content.value_statement: Developer relations teams can spread limited capacity across activities without a clear business purpose. This skill guides interviews and decisions into a focused, reviewable charter.
actual_capabilities: Conduct a guided interview to establish the funding driver, deadline, capacity, budget ownership, and planning horizon.
Structure a CORE analysis covering community, organization, relationships, and ecosystem.
Compare program archetypes and select two primary goals plus one secondary goal tied to developer journey problems.
Prioritize an audience and choose in-house, contractor, agency, or community sourcing for each proposed initiative.
Define the next staffing capability and its hiring trigger without creating a full organization chart.
Draft a twelve-section charter with owners, signals, review dates, explicit exclusions, open questions, and an executive narrative.
limitations: Does not produce tactical content, event plans, a first-90-days execution plan, or a complete measurement framework.
Does not calculate detailed budgets, reporting lines, or staffing ratios; it refers those decisions to related skills.
Recommendations depend on accurate user inputs; numeric capacity and prioritization rules are adjustable starting baselines, not validated industry standards.
Persistent context storage and public-source browsing depend on the host environment; users should control what business information is retained.

use_cases.title: Start a funded program
use_cases.description: Identify the sponsor, audience, initial priorities, and capacity limits before committing to new developer relations activities.
use_cases.target_user: First DevRel hire at an API startup

use_cases.title: Refocus an overloaded team
use_cases.description: Replace an expanding activity list with a small set of funded initiatives, clear exclusions, and a justified next capability.

use_cases.title: Prepare for an executive review
use_cases.description: Connect program investment to observable developer problems and prepare an executive narrative with review dates and unresolved assumptions.

prompt_templates.title: Begin the strategy interview
prompt_templates.prompt: We are starting DevRel for [product] with [team capacity]. Interview me one question at a time to establish our funding driver and constraints.

prompt_templates.title: Compare program directions
prompt_templates.prompt: Our sponsor wants [outcome] by [date]. Developers struggle at [journey step]. Compare feasible program archetypes for [capacity] and explain their trade-offs.

prompt_templates.title: Choose sourcing and staffing
prompt_templates.prompt: Our chosen direction is [archetype], with initiatives [list]. Compare sourcing options, retain credibility-sensitive work internally, and propose the next capability with its trigger.
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced: align delivery choices with capacity.

prompt_templates.title: Build and challenge the charter
prompt_templates.prompt: Using [program context], develop our charter section by section. Check goal traceability, capacity, sourcing, exclusions, and review triggers. Label assumptions and adjustable baselines.

output_examples.input: Illustrative scenario: one advocate, strong signups, weak second-use activation, and a ten-week executive review deadline.
output: Direction: enablement-first, subject to confirming the sponsor and capacity.
Initial initiative: improve the quickstart. Owner: advocate. Signal: second successful use. Review: week eight.
Sourcing: retain technical decisions and review internally; exclude a new agency pipeline because setup exceeds the deadline.
Excluded: conference sponsorship and a new community venue until activation improves.

output_examples.input: Illustrative scenario: enterprise technical evaluations stall; the revenue leader sponsors two DevRel practitioners.
output: Driver: sales enablement. Sponsor: revenue leader.
Direction: evaluation-support for platform engineers whose deployments require an approver.
Candidate initiatives: scoped proof-of-concept material, reference architectures, and reusable security and licensing answers.
Next capability: technical writing, triggered by a sustained review backlog.
Open question: establish the evaluation drop-off baseline before selecting a success target.

best_practices: Confirm the funding owner, deadline, capacity, and budget scope before selecting activities.
Connect every initiative to a primary goal, named owner, observable signal, and review date.
Label assumptions and adjustable baselines, and review the charter when the sponsor or product context changes.
anti_patterns: Copying a large company by spreading a small team evenly across all four pillars.
Treating a calendar of posts, events, and community launches as a strategy without observed developer problems.
Outsourcing technical judgment, incident communication, or advocacy voice to increase output.

faq.question: What does this skill produce?
faq.answer: It produces a short DevRel charter covering position, funding, goals, audience, priorities, sourcing, staffing, exclusions, open questions, executive messaging, and review.

faq.question: What information should I provide?
faq.answer: Provide your product, adoption path, sponsor, team capacity, existing assets, budget scope, deadline, and constraints. The skill asks clarifying questions.

faq.question: Does it create detailed budgets or dashboards?
faq.answer: No. It assigns one signal per initiative and refers detailed budget allocation, measurement frameworks, and organization design to related skills.

faq.question: Are its numeric rules industry benchmarks?
faq.answer: No. Capacity limits and goal counts are adjustable starting baselines. Historical survey figures require attribution and should not become automatic targets.

faq.question: Does it require web access or save business context?
faq.answer: Browsing is optional for checking public references. It requests context storage in available memory or a local file; avoid retaining sensitive information.

faq.question: Can I use it with Claude, Codex, or Claude Code?
faq.answer: The skill declares support for all three. Available browsing and persistence features depend on the host environment.
